Baltimore bills as a city, not a county

Baltimore has been an independent city since 1851. Baltimore County surrounds it, but the two are separate governments, so no county bill sits on top of the city's. The 2020 census counted 585,708 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 569,997. Housing is mostly rowhouses, many with brick or formstone fronts, and many blocks fall in historic districts, which can limit exterior work. Ask before you assume a quick cosmetic fix is allowed.

One city bill carries the city rate and the state rate together, and the office that collects it also runs the annual tax sale. A tax balance here deserves attention early.

Rates and how a bill is figured

The city rate is $2.248 per $100 of assessed value, and the state adds $0.112 per $100 on the same bill, which the city forwards to the state. The combined rate is $2.360 per $100. The state assessments office, SDAT, sets each parcel's value, and the city applies its rate to that figure. The budget office's tax-rate page shows $2.248 for fiscal 2027.

Tax or creditRate or limit
City real property rate$2.248 per $100 of assessed value
State rate on the city bill$0.112 per $100
Combined$2.360 per $100
Homestead credit cap, from July 1, 20264% a year on a principal residence
City transfer tax1.5% of the cash consideration
Recordation tax$5.00 per $500 of consideration paid

Transfer and recordation taxes yield less on sales over $1 million, and part of each goes to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund. Your sales contract decides who pays at closing.

The 2026 reassessment and the homestead cap

Baltimore was in Maryland's Group 2 reassessment, and residential full cash value rose 13.4% between January 1, 2023 and January 1, 2026. Increases phase in evenly over three years, and decreases apply in full for the 2026 tax year. If you live in the house and have applied for the homestead credit, the 4% cap means a big jump in market value does not become a big jump in taxable value right away.

If you inherited a house or moved out years ago, check whether the credit is still attached. It needs a principal residence, so a rental or empty house can lose the cap and see the taxable value catch up faster.

Due dates, interest and the tax sale

Bills are mailed July 1 and are due on receipt, with a half-percent discount if paid by July 31. After October 1, unpaid tax accrues 1% interest plus a 1% monthly penalty. Owner-occupied homes and small businesses with taxes under $100,000 can pay in two equal installments, with a small fee added to the second. A pending appeal does not excuse a late payment, but a successful one produces a refund with interest.

A property becomes eligible for the annual tax sale when it is behind by at least $750 on an owner-occupied residence or $250 on a non-owner-occupied one.

  • First week of February: Final Bill and Legal Notice mailed to the address in land records.
  • First week of April: second letter.
  • May: the online tax sale.
  • First week of July: post-sale informational letter.

You can stop a sale by redeeming, which means paying the winning bidder all claims, interest and costs. A Tax Sale Deferral Program run through Finance and Housing and Community Development can keep a property out of the sale for a year.

Other city charges that become liens

Unpaid annual registration fees on non-owner-occupied property are a lien and can go to tax sale. They surprise many sellers, since the fees are small and easy to miss on a rental or an inherited vacant house.

  • 1- and 2-family dwellings: $30 per dwelling unit.
  • Multifamily dwellings: $35 per dwelling unit or $25 per rooming unit.
  • Vacant residential structures: $100 per structure plus $30 per dwelling unit.
  • Vacant lots: $25 per lot.

Owners of registered vacant buildings must keep them clean and secure until they are razed or rehabilitated, and the city bills the owner if it does the work first. A 2024 state law also lets the City Council set a special tax rate on abandoned properties. Call the city to learn whether a rate applies to your parcel.

Weather, flooding and older rowhouses

Elevation ranges from sea level at the harbor to about 480 feet in the northwest. Lower blocks near the water see more flooding, while hillside neighborhoods deal with drainage and old foundations. Buyers and inspectors look hard at basements, rear additions and roofs on rowhouses after a wet year, so gather any repair records before you list.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What closing looks like with a city balance

At settlement the title company totals the city payoff, any registration fees and the transfer and recordation taxes your contract assigns to you. The payoff must be good through the closing date, which is why a figure requested weeks earlier may be too low once interest or penalties keep accruing. Ask for an updated number a few days before you sign.

Vacant houses draw extra attention. The housing department reported 13,411 vacant building notices as of mid-2024, 863 of them on city-owned property, so a boarded-up house you own may already be on a list. Keep it clean and secure, and resolve any registration charges before the sale so they do not delay the title work.

If the house has been in the family for years and the paperwork is a mess, tell the title company at the start. Sorting out who is the owner of record can take longer than paying the bill.

First steps when taxes are due

Find out what you owe and whether the property is marked for the May sale. The collections call center is 410-396-3000, and assessment questions and credits go to the state office at 410-767-8250.

  1. Pull the current bill on the city payment site and note any balance from earlier years.
  2. Check for registration or other city charges on the account.
  3. Ask for a payoff figure good through your expected closing date.
  4. Tell the title company early so the payoff is built into the settlement statement.

If money is tight, a payment plan or the deferral program may buy time. When the house also needs work and the balance keeps growing, selling as is for cash can clear the lien from the proceeds at closing. Call or text us with the address and we will tell you what we can offer.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Baltimore City property tax rate?

The city rate is $2.248 per $100 of assessed value, and the state adds $0.112 per $100 on the same bill. That is $2.360 combined, before any credits.

Does Baltimore property tax jump when my house is reassessed?

Not all at once for most owners. Increases phase in over three years, and a principal residence with the homestead credit is capped at 4% a year from July 1, 2026.

How much unpaid tax puts a Baltimore house into the tax sale?

A property becomes eligible once it is delinquent by at least $750 for an owner-occupied residence or $250 for other property. The sale is held online each May after notices in February and April.

Can I sell a Baltimore house that is already in the tax sale process?

Usually yes, but timing matters. Owners can stop a sale by redeeming, so ask the collections office for a payoff figure and tell your title company right away.

What are the Baltimore transfer and recordation taxes?

The city transfer tax is 1.5% of the cash consideration, and the recordation tax is $5.00 per $500 of consideration. Who pays each is set in the contract.

Selling in the city of Frederick

Frederick is where Frederick County's government sits, about 46 miles from Baltimore heading west and 50 miles from Washington, D.C. heading north. The city counted 78,171 people in 2020 and an estimated 92,059 by 2025.

Newer development surrounds a compact, walkable historic core, and that core is where most preservation rules apply. Interstates 70 and 270, U.S. 15 and U.S. 340 meet here, and MARC commuter rail and express bus 991 to the Shady Grove Metro station serve commuters, so buyers who work in the Washington area treat Frederick as a realistic home base. The area's biggest employer is Fort Detrick, at 10,827 jobs.

The city tax rate

Inside city limits, the fiscal 2025 state figures put the total real property rate at 1.7382 for every $100 of assessed value, split between a county piece and a city piece.

Part of the bill (fiscal 2025)Rate per $100 of assessed value
County rate inside the city1.0077
City rate0.7305
Combined1.7382
Unincorporated Frederick County, for reference1.1100

The city share funds street maintenance, trash removal and police. Homestead credit caps differ town to town, from 0 percent up to 10 percent. A city address costs more per $100 than a county one, so buyers comparing Frederick with nearby areas will ask for the full bill. Keep a copy handy. Show how the bill splits between county and city, because many buyers assume the county number alone is the whole bill and are surprised by the city line.

Due dates and discounts

County Treasury sets September 30 as the due date for annual bills and first installments, and December 31 for second installments. From October 1, an unpaid account gains 1 percent a month. A July payment gets a 1 percent discount, and an August payment gets half of one percent.

You can reach Treasury at 30 North Market Street or 301-600-1111, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. SDAT, which sets the assessed value, answers at 301-815-5350.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your assessment

SDAT sets a new value about every third year. If yours looks off, appeal in this order:

  1. Supervisor of Assessments: 45 days from the notice date.
  2. Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board: 30 days after that decision.
  3. Maryland Tax Court: 30 days after the board's order.

Two credits are worth asking about. The Senior Tax Credit takes 20 percent off net county real property taxes for owners 65 or older within the income limits. The Homestead Tax Credit puts a ceiling on yearly increases in the taxable value of a principal residence.

Older neighborhoods and downtown

The Frederick Historic District holds more than 200 retailers, restaurants and antique shops along Market, Patrick and East Streets, and about 600 businesses and organizations operate downtown. First Saturday draws about 11,000 people on average each month. West Patrick Street follows the old National Road, now U.S. 40, and Culler Lake is a man-made lake in the middle of town.

Daniel Dulany laid out the town by 1745, and Schifferstadt, built in 1756, is probably the oldest surviving house in the city. Older houses near the core often come with preservation review, mixed-age systems and surprises behind the walls. A seller who has permits, repair receipts and a recent inspection report on hand gives buyers fewer reasons to pause or ask for a lower price.

Historic district and exterior work rules

Before changing the outside of a designated site, or a property in a Historic Preservation Overlay district, you must get a certificate of approval from the Historic Preservation Commission. The commission reviews exterior features only, never interior layout. A home sale does not need its approval, but a buyer who plans a new porch, windows or siding will.

  • Changes need review even when they cannot be seen from the street. Routine maintenance and landscaping with no material effect are exempt.
  • The commission has 45 days to act on a complete application. If it does not act, the application is approved unless the applicant agrees to more time.
  • A certificate expires after three years without a building or zoning permit, with one six-month extension.
  • A decision can be challenged in the Circuit Court for Frederick County, within 30 days.

Outside the overlay, a plan can still face demolition review when it removes more than 25 percent of floor area, changes significant roof lines or moves the structure. Tell your agent or buyer about any pending exterior plans early.

When you are selling, a short list helps. Gather the certificate of approval for any past exterior change, the building or zoning permit that went with it and any notice of violation that was closed. A house with gaps in that paper trail can lose a financed buyer late in the process, because the lender or the buyer's inspector will notice work that was never approved. If something is missing, ask the city's historic preservation staff how to resolve it before the house is listed rather than after a contract is signed.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Carroll Creek and flood questions

Downtown has a flood history, and the Carroll Creek flood control project was built to reduce flood risk from the 100-year floodplain. A Carroll Creek Overlay District in the city code sets design standards for new construction and rehabilitation near the creek. Buyers of a house near the creek will ask about the floodplain and the overlay standards. City planning staff can supply those answers before you list.

Selling with back taxes

Back tax is no barrier to selling, since your title company can pay it out of the sale money. The only real work is getting the figure right, and the earlier you start, the fewer surprises appear at the settlement table.

  1. Order a Lien Certificate or Tax Status Report through Treasury.
  2. Check for a separate city district tax or supplemental bill.
  3. Give the amounts to the title company before you set the closing date, since interest of 1 percent a month keeps adding to the balance.
  4. Pay the county and any city bill at closing from proceeds, then keep the receipts with your sale papers.

Landlords should know that city inspectors, reachable at 301-600-3825, handle rental condition complaints for properties inside the city, so check for open ones before listing. A cash buyer will take a house that needs work as-is, and the tax payoff is simply settled at closing. Before any of that, make sure your mailing address on file with Treasury is current, because a missed notice does not stop interest from running and can leave you with a larger payoff than you expected.

Frequently asked questions

How high is the Frederick city tax rate?

The fiscal 2025 state table shows 1.7382 per $100 inside the city, made up of a 1.0077 county rate and a 0.7305 city rate. Rates reset yearly, so check your current notice.

When is Frederick property tax due?

Annual bills and first installments are due September 30, second installments December 31. Late balances grow 1 percent a month from October 1, while a July payment saves 1 percent.

Who do I call about my Frederick property tax?

Call the County Treasury at 301-600-1111 for billing, and SDAT at 301-815-5350 for the assessed value. Treasury is at 30 North Market Street.

Does the Historic Preservation Commission review a house sale?

No. Exterior work on a designated or overlay property needs approval, and the commission has 45 days to act on a complete application.

Can I sell with back taxes owed?

Yes. Your proceeds cover it at closing, paid by the title company. Pull a lien certificate or tax status report from Treasury first to learn the exact amount before choosing a date.
